lxc_084263cd02c50e3a.text: Chapulines, anticuchos, natto, stinky tofu, mopane worms, and kitfo look strange to many first-time eaters, but each one is an everyday food with a clear reason behind the mix.

lxc_ee0c92e975d24cb7.text: Three simple questions explain them: where the food comes from, how people change it, and what the finished dish tastes like.

lxc_56315600c05eb011.text: Many surprising foods start with a simple idea: use what is around you, then change it with heat and strong seasoning.

lxc_4afdd0345847d402.text: In Latin America, two street foods show this clearly.

lxc_302a99ddf73e3e0a.text: Chapulines are grasshoppers eaten in parts of Mexico and Central America.

lxc_565fbee812d17d5d.text: The name comes from Nahuatl, an old language of Mexico, and Spanish records from the early to mid-16th century already mention grasshoppers as food.

lxc_c003db900ee8c431.text: Oaxaca is the main region, but they are also popular near Mexico City, Tepoztlán, Cuernavaca, and Puebla.

lxc_6b2fcb10358cbf06.text: The insect itself is the source; the change is toasting them and seasoning with garlic, lime juice, chilies, or salt.

lxc_0c119bb95330522b.text: The result is a crunchy, salty, sour snack, or a filling for a large tortilla dish called a tlayuda.

lxc_83ec6c501f06aa8b.text: Anticuchos come from the Andes, especially Peru, and also Bolivia, Chile, and Ecuador.

lxc_59b4d38be2eb31b4.text: The most popular version uses beef heart.

lxc_7421b8d51a1aef4d.text: In colonial times, Spanish households valued organ cuts less, so these cheap cuts became common in street food, and today people across Peru eat anticuchos.

lxc_efa968be89aa5a73.text: The heart is marinated in vinegar and spices such as cumin, aji pepper, and garlic, then grilled on a skewer, often with a boiled potato at the end.

lxc_1e728e3de54e274d.text: The strong marinade and smoky grill change a cheap cut into something people line up for.

lxc_f1141e09420627f2.text: In Asia, the surprise often comes not from the ingredient but from the change.

lxc_a3f760e710be4d61.text: Both natto and stinky tofu begin with soybeans, a very ordinary food, and both are fermented, which means bacteria or other tiny organisms slowly change the food over time.

lxc_e3d16041d610eac5.text: Fermentation creates the smell that shocks newcomers and the flavor that fans love.

lxc_7f5fa5b33c0f79eb.text: Natto is whole soybeans fermented with a bacterium called Bacillus subtilis var.

lxc_9db7833d0d6cdc24.text: In eastern Japan, including Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokkaido, many people eat it for breakfast on rice with mustard, soy sauce, and spring onion.

lxc_a0d7d63b6f8d5229.text: The change gives it a strong smell, a sticky texture with long strings, and a strong taste.

lxc_f8e0fbc6234b722d.text: Many call it an acquired taste, yet a 2009 survey found about 70 percent of respondents liked it.

lxc_1e875a17dc83effe.text: So a food that looks difficult is, for most people in its home region, simply a normal morning meal.

lxc_ac530efdf5d60d2a.text: Stinky tofu is Chinese fermented tofu, a famous night-market snack in Taiwan and common in many parts of China.

lxc_31c740211a3d4280.text: A legend says Wang Zhihe made an early version in the Qing dynasty after leftover tofu fermented in a jar.

lxc_34cdc1871d0bc0bb.text: People compare the smell to strong cheese or even garbage, but the taste is usually milder and savory.

lxc_713a9ad852430f19.text: It can be steamed, stewed, or grilled, though fried stinky tofu is the night-market favorite, and fans say the smellier batches often taste better.

lxc_70c8a587e2d4ca9b.text: In Africa, two dishes show a different kind of contrast: one is a wild insect turned into a shelf-stable food, and the other is fresh raw meat made rich with spice and butter.

lxc_ee9183a6a2c7e23a.text: Mopane worms are large caterpillars of the moth Gonimbrasia belina, common in warmer southern Africa.

lxc_e6e17cebfb94867a.text: They feed mainly on the leaves of the mopane tree, and they are an important source of protein in the region.

lxc_79c664051b925574.text: After cleaning, people boil them with salt and then dry or smoke them.

lxc_42c099f03167bc83.text: The change matters: drying turns a soft caterpillar into a crunchy snack that keeps for a long time, or it can be cooked again with onion, tomato, and spices.

lxc_166dc69a53058935.text: Because they keep well, they are traded across countries such as Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe.

lxc_4946d664055fa7bc.text: Kitfo is an Ethiopian dish from Gurage tradition, made of minced raw beef.

lxc_aaf72f386c923572.text: Here the change is not heat but seasoning: the meat is mixed with mitmita, a hot chili spice powder, and niter kibbeh, a spiced clarified butter.

lxc_1a5f93464e0b4020.text: When it is cooked lightly rare, it is called kitfo leb leb.

lxc_3124a008340c6148.text: It is often served with ayibe, a mild cheese, or gomen, cooked greens, together with injera flatbread or, among Gurage cooks, with kocho.

lxc_0321022a212fd5f5.text: Kitfo appears on special days such as the feast of Meskel, so the raw meat that surprises visitors is, for many Ethiopians, a celebration food.
